To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

hippocampal LFPs and neural activity reflect the temporal topography and the behavioral significance of conditioned responses, respectively, and that the hippocampal LTFs are a result of the interaction between the cerebellum and the hippocampus.

hippocampal participation is required for the acquisition of complex classical conditioning, and that the hippocampus may be involved in regulating the contents of the limited capacity STM that is used to store the conditioned stimulus (CS), unconditioned stimulus(US) association.

(a) the hippocampus participates in classical conditioning, but not as the site where associations between CS and US are formed; (b) the hippocampus regulates the STM contents of the cerebellum during learning, and this regulation depends on afferents from the cerebellum to the hippocampus; and (c) the hippocampus also participates in the storage of CS-US associations in long-term memory (LTM), and this participation depends on the integrity and functional state of the hippocampus.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the following issues: (a) the role of the hippocampus in classical conditioning, (b) the role of cerebellar-cortical circuits in classical conditioning, and the (c) role of the hippocampal-cortical circuits.
